# Maite Sorell Valdeza

**Curriculum vitae — updated 24 September 2026**

Department of Language and Public Institutions, Universidad de Valdencina, Zaragoza, Spain.

## Appointment and qualifications

I hold a permanent appointment as Profesora Titular de Universidad in applied linguistics at Universidad de Valdencina, a Spanish public university. The appointment began on 1 September 2018 and has no contractual end date. I obtained national accreditation for this category in 2017.

My qualifications, all awarded by Universidad de Valdencina, are a degree in Spanish Philology, completed in 2006; a master's degree in discourse research, completed in 2008; and a PhD in Applied Linguistics, awarded in 2012. My doctoral dissertation examined comprehension and repair in municipal service encounters.

Following my doctorate, I held a university postdoctoral research appointment from 2012 to 2015 and a fixed-term lecturer appointment from 2015 to 2018. My current responsibilities combine undergraduate teaching, research, postgraduate supervision and departmental service. My allocated teaching for the 2025–2026 academic year was 160 contact hours, covering discourse analysis, institutional communication and research methods. I have two recognised six-year research periods, covering 2012–2017 and 2018–2023; the second was recognised in 2024.

## Research experience and funded responsibilities

My research examines how people understand service information, formulate requests and recover from misunderstandings in public institutions. I combine interactional analysis, interviews, document analysis and repeated measures of comprehension. Language access is examined through the relationships between users, documents, staff practices and institutional rules.

From 2017 to 2019, I was principal investigator of *Understanding municipal appointment letters*, supported by the Universidad de Valdencina internal research programme. I was responsible for its research design, ethics submission, analysis and final report. The study involved collaboration with municipal staff on the wording of appointment instructions and the procedural obligations those instructions conveyed.

From 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025, I led the language-assessment work package in *Palabras de ventanilla y cuidados rurales*, funded by the regional Programa Aragonés de Investigación sobre Servicios de Proximidad, award PAISP-2022-017. I developed the assessment rubric, coordinated interviewer training, supervised paired-score analysis and led preparation of the language findings. Dr Berta Lascuén Aroza, Instituto de Estudios Cívicos de Valdemora, was overall scientific coordinator and was responsible for the consolidated project report.

## Publications, supervision and methods

My full publication record comprises 14 peer-reviewed articles and 5 book chapters. The accompanying selected publications list contains five articles from the service-language research line. Other outputs concern interactional repair, institutional discourse and methods of analysing public-service documents.

I currently supervise Elena Valtuerña Saz, enrolled as a doctoral researcher since October 2023. Her dissertation examines repair sequences in rural service interviews. Her work includes supervised coding, transcript checking and documentation of analytic decisions; her doctorate remains in progress.

My completed empirical work comprises observational studies, qualitative analyses and instrument development. I have experience coordinating interview consent procedures with older adults and integrating language findings with nursing and administrative-law interpretation.

# Final scientific summary: Palabras de ventanilla y cuidados rurales

**Issued 18 March 2026; administrative status checked 24 September 2026**

Project period: 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025. Funding: Programa Aragonés de Investigación sobre Servicios de Proximidad, regional award PAISP-2022-017. Total awarded funding: EUR 184,000, comprising EUR 120,000 administered by Instituto de Estudios Cívicos de Valdemora and EUR 64,000 administered by Universidad de Valdencina.

Overall scientific coordinator: Dr Berta Lascuén Aroza, Instituto de Estudios Cívicos de Valdemora. Language-assessment work-package lead: Dr Maite Sorell Valdeza, Universidad de Valdencina. The project is complete. The regional office acknowledged receipt of the consolidated final report in March 2026.

## Purpose and setting

The project examined service language, administrative procedures and the practical work older rural residents undertake when seeking care-related information. Its empirical focus was residents' accounts of encounters and their ability to interpret information about an appointment, a supporting document or a referral.

Participating centres were local service points providing care-related information, nursing contact or administrative assistance. Their functions included both community-facing advice and care coordination. Access was negotiated separately at each centre. The coordinating institute managed cross-institution administration; the university managed the language instruments and the university-held interview corpus.

## Sample and procedures

The completed 2025 field study interviewed 90 rural residents aged 65 or older across 15 service centres. Recruitment was purposive, with six interviewees at each centre. Centre staff circulated the approved information sheet, and researchers documented individual consent before enrolment. Participants were able to undertake an interview with the communication support available under the approved protocol.

Interviews were completed between February and May 2025. Each participant discussed a recent service encounter and completed an initial language-access assessment. A repeat assessment was offered four to six weeks later to examine score change across the participant's next routine centre contact. Routine contact could include explanation of an appointment, document requirement or referral. Staff explanations were not standardised, and the research team did not allocate an intervention. All repeat assessments were complete by July 2025.

The repeated task used equivalent service scenarios. Interviewers recorded participants' accounts of the intervening contact, but there was no independent verification of the content or duration of staff assistance. The assessment concerned interpretation of service information rather than whether treatment or an entitlement had been obtained.

Paired assessments were available for 72 participants, representing 80% of the interview sample. Of the remaining 18 participants, 11 declined the repeat assessment and seven could not be reached within the follow-up window. All initial interviews and assessments were retained under the participants' consent. No missing follow-up scores were imputed for the primary descriptive analysis.

## Instrument and analysis

The language-access score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating more successful interpretation and explanation of service information. Tasks covered identifying a required action, understanding a deadline, distinguishing a recommendation from a requirement, and explaining where clarification could be sought. The rubric was developed within the project; validation against health literacy, completed care access or wellbeing measures was not undertaken.

Two assessors independently scored 32 of the 162 assessment records before discussion of disagreements: 16 initial and 16 repeat assessments, selected across centres. Absolute-agreement reliability for a single assessor, estimated using a two-way random-effects intraclass correlation coefficient, was ICC 0.86 (95% CI 0.73–0.93). The scoring manual records the subsequent consensus decisions used in the analytic dataset.

The paired analysis estimated mean within-person score change among completers. Its confidence interval used resampling at centre level to reflect clustering. With only 15 centres, the interval remains sensitive to the observed centres. It describes sampling uncertainty under the analysis assumptions and excludes uncertainty from selection bias, differential attrition and unmeasured changes between assessments.

Two researchers independently coded 18 interviews before reconciliation. Cohen's kappa was 0.78 for language-related difficulties, 0.77 for administrative sequencing and 0.75 for transport. Interview-resampled 95% confidence intervals were 0.44–1.00, 0.42–1.00 and 0.36–1.00, respectively. These wide intervals reflect the small reliability subsample. Final counts use reconciled coding and the resulting definitions applied to the full corpus. Digital procedures were not coded as a separate category.

## Findings

Among the 72 participants with paired observations, the mean initial score was 52 and the mean repeat score was 58. Mean within-person change was 6 points on the 0–100 scale, with a 95% confidence interval of 2 to 10 points.

The initial mean among the 18 non-completers was 49, compared with 52 among completers; the initial mean across all 90 participants was 51.4. This descriptive comparison indicates that the retained group began with somewhat higher scores. It does not establish whether the missing repeat assessments would have increased or reduced the estimated change.

Qualitative coding identified language-related difficulties in 54 interviews, administrative-sequencing difficulties in 41 and transport-related difficulties in 37. These are non-exclusive counts from the 90 interviews. A mention counted when a participant described a concrete encounter or obstacle. The counts characterise the collected narratives rather than population prevalence.

A correctly understood instruction could still be difficult to act on when a resident lacked transport, needed another document or could not identify the responsible office. Staff explanation sometimes resolved an immediate misunderstanding while the underlying procedure remained unchanged. These observations informed the distinction between comprehension, procedural burden and service outcome in the final coding framework.

## Limitations and completed outputs

The score change is observational. There was no random assignment, untreated comparison group or standardised language-support intervention. Equivalent scenarios reduced direct recall but did not remove task familiarisation. Routine staff help, other intervening experiences and selective follow-up could all contribute to the observed change. The result does not establish a causal care-access benefit.

The purposive sample is not population-representative and missed residents with no contact with participating centres. Interviews were not linked to clinical records, completed referrals were not independently verified, and changes in wellbeing were not measured.

Cultural participation was not a structured exposure. References to libraries, associations or local events arose incidentally, without a common question sequence or reliable denominator. No cultural intervention took place.

Completed outputs include a restricted interview corpus, scoring rubric, coding manual, published analyses and an aggregate feedback note returned to participating service managers. Receipt of that note was documented; implementation was not evaluated. Public materials comprise blank instruments, the codebook and disclosure-checked aggregate tables.

# Selected publications from the service-language research line

**Verified list, 24 September 2026**

The five published articles below are selected from Maite Sorell Valdeza's wider publication record. Titles, author order and identifiers follow the final published records. Contribution notes record the division of work within this research line.

## Published articles

**Sorell Valdeza, M. (2016). Repair sequences in municipal information encounters: an interactional account. Journal of Institutional Language Practices.**

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-rural-service-language-team.2016.1

This article examines how residents and staff identify and repair misunderstandings during municipal information encounters. It draws on the author's doctoral and postdoctoral research. Its contribution is an analytic distinction between identifying an unfamiliar expression and resolving uncertainty about the next administrative action. Sorell Valdeza conducted the analysis and prepared the manuscript. The article established the interactional categories subsequently used in the team's work on service instructions.

**Sorell Valdeza, M., and Brizuela Laredo, T. (2019). When an appointment letter becomes an administrative barrier: comprehension and procedural obligations. Review of Language and Administrative Practice.**

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-rural-service-language-team.2019.2

This article reports the internally supported study led by Sorell Valdeza. It combines linguistic analysis of appointment letters with legal analysis of the obligations represented in them. The analysis distinguishes interpreting an instruction from satisfying its procedural requirements. Sorell Valdeza led the empirical work; Brizuela Laredo examined relationships between wording, procedural duties and information rights.

**Sorell Valdeza, M., Nereda Soláns, A., and Lascuén Aroza, B. (2023). Separating comprehension from service access in rural care communication research. Studies in Rural Service Encounters.**

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-rural-service-language-team.2023.3

This methodological article establishes the predecessor project's measurement distinctions. Published before the 2025 field study, it develops a framework for distinguishing comprehension, practical completion of administrative steps and receipt of care. Nereda Soláns contributed nursing interpretation of care pathways. Lascuén Aroza contributed the public-service research framework as overall project coordinator.

**Sorell Valdeza, M., Nereda Soláns, A., and Valtuerña Saz, E. (2026). Repeated language-access assessments among older rural service users: an observational study. Journal of Public Service Comprehension.**

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-rural-service-language-team.2026.4

Published in March 2026, this article reports the paired assessment analysis summarised in the final project report, including the baseline comparison of completers and non-completers and the assessment reliability exercise. Sorell Valdeza led the analysis and manuscript; Nereda Soláns reviewed interpretation of care-related scenarios; Valtuerña Saz contributed supervised data checking and documentation of coding decisions.

**Sorell Valdeza, M., Brizuela Laredo, T., and Cendal Orduña, R. (2026). Language, paperwork and travel in older residents' accounts of rural care services. Review of Territorial Service Research.**

DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-rural-service-language-team.2026.5

Published in June 2026, this article integrates interview coding with analysis of administrative sequences using the predecessor project's interview sample. Brizuela Laredo analysed procedural obligations. Cendal Orduña mapped local service responsibilities and reviewed the interpretation of institutional procedures. The article examines how linguistic, administrative and territorial difficulties intersect within residents' accounts.

## University team

**Dr Maite Sorell Valdeza — applied linguistics.** Profesora Titular de Universidad and the team's scientific coordinator at Universidad de Valdencina. **Dr Tomás Brizuela Laredo — administrative law.** Permanent lecturer at the same university. His research concerns procedural obligations, access to public information and the practical completion of administrative processes. He analysed the predecessor project's service documents and contributes to interpretation of the institutional requirements described in interviews.

Her doctorate is in progress. Her assigned duties are supervised coding, transcript checks and research documentation, under Sorell Valdeza's supervision.

## Established public-administration collaboration

Dr Rocío Cendal Orduña is a public-administration researcher at Instituto de Estudios Cívicos de Valdemora. She contributed to the completed project and is a co-author of the June 2026 analysis. The institute and university have an active collaboration agreement covering scholarly exchange and authorised analysis of the completed study.

Cendal Orduña maps responsibilities across local service offices and reviews whether descriptions of procedures reflect their institutional setting. The agreement specifies scholarly exchange, interpretation of service procedures and access to approved research materials under the corpus governance arrangements. Site entry and access to personal service records are handled through separate permissions.

## Facilities already available

The university provides an access-controlled audio repository, an institutionally managed transcription workstation and encrypted storage for consent records. Transcription takes place within the university's secure environment. Named accounts and approved roles govern access, and changes to access are logged. Consent records and the linkage key are stored separately from analytic files.

The team has current access to statistical software, qualitative coding software and university-managed version control for scripts and codebooks. The project archive includes the scoring rubric, interviewer instructions, coding definitions and a record of analysis decisions. The university's research support office assists with agreements and information governance.

The archive supports joint review of coding decisions: analysts retain dated codebook versions, record reasons for changes and preserve the scripts used to generate aggregate tables. Disclosure review precedes circulation of quotations or tabulations outside the authorised research group.

# Interview corpus and access protocol

**University research governance memorandum, 24 September 2026**

Custodian: Dr Maite Sorell Valdeza, Universidad de Valdencina. This memorandum records the permissions attached to the completed rural service-language study, the materials retained and the institutional procedure for site access and participant enrolment.

## Existing permissions and materials

The university ethics committee approved the predecessor study under reference UV-CEI-2024-041 on 12 December 2024. Written site permissions covered the 15 participating service centres. Each of the 90 interview participants gave documented informed consent before enrolment, including consent to the interview, its recording, the assessments and the specified research use of the material.

The approved information sheet and consent process covered subsequent analysis of the interview corpus concerning language, administrative and territorial barriers in care-related service encounters. Secondary analysis within this scope is covered by UV-CEI-2024-041 and requires no further approval. This authorisation excludes new interviews, recontact for a different study, linkage to clinical records and unrestricted changes of research purpose.

The restricted corpus contains 90 interview transcripts and their associated audio, initial assessment records for all 90 participants and repeat assessment records for 72 participants. There are 162 assessment records in total. The 18 participants without repeat assessments remain represented by their initial assessments and interviews. Analytic files contain pseudonymous centre codes and research identifiers. Names and contact details are held separately. Access to the linkage key is limited to the designated custodian and authorised governance staff.

Some interviews contain incidental references to cultural or associational activities. The consent documents cover the approved service-encounter research purpose. They do not provide consent for a separate cultural-participation study. A material change of purpose requires a documented governance assessment and, where applicable, an ethics amendment or additional consent. The incidental references were collected without a common participation instrument and cannot constitute a validated participation measure.

## Site and consent registers

At 24 September 2026, the permission register contains entries only for the 15 centres under UV-CEI-2024-041. The consent register contains only the records of the 90 participants in that study. No new-site application or ethics amendment is on file. Existing site permissions apply to the named centres and the approved study.

## Procedure for new sites and participants

The institutional protocol prohibits recruitment into a new-centre study before both written permission from that centre and the person's documented informed consent are in place. Written permission must identify the authorised activity and the responsible site contact. Informal introductions and expressions of interest are recorded as correspondence, separately from the permission register.

Following written site permission and the applicable ethics approval, authorised site staff may circulate an approved information sheet. This information stage precedes enrolment. Researchers must provide an accessible explanation, establish that participation is voluntary and document consent before the person is recruited into the research sample or any research interview or assessment begins. Access to services must not depend on participation.

The protocol requires communication support appropriate to the person and a check that the explanation has been understood. Older age alone is not evidence of impaired decision-making capacity. Inclusion through proxy consent requires separate approved arrangements; the existing procedure covers participants providing their own consent.

## Storage, disclosure and analysis

Audio, transcripts and assessment files remain restricted. Pseudonymisation does not make them anonymous: combinations of village, service encounter and family circumstances can identify someone locally. Analysts remove unnecessary identifiers and review distinctive contextual details before using quotations. The custodian maintains the access register and records the purpose of each approved analyst's access.

The approved retention schedule permits restricted storage through 31 December 2030, followed by documented deletion or a separately authorised retention decision. Original consent records and governance documentation follow the university's applicable records schedule. Participants received a contact route for questions and requests concerning their data.

Publicly shareable materials comprise blank instruments, the codebook and disclosure-checked aggregate results. Individual-level files remain restricted. External collaborators receive access only after approval of their role, purpose and confidentiality obligations. Shared outputs are checked for small-cell disclosure and identifying combinations of contextual details before release.

Its confidence interval used resampling at centre level to reflect the clustering of participants within the participating centres. The limited number of centres constrains the precision of this procedure. The interval describes sampling uncertainty under the analysis assumptions; it does not account for selection bias, differential attrition or unmeasured changes between assessments.

## Findings

Among the 72 participants with paired observations, the mean initial score was 52 and the mean repeat score was 58. Mean improvement was 6 points on the 0–100 scale, with a 95% confidence interval of 2 to 10 points. This is an observational within-person change. It is not evidence that language support caused better access to care.

Qualitative coding identified language-related difficulties in 54 interviews, administrative-sequencing difficulties in 41 and transport-related difficulties in 37. These are non-exclusive counts from the 90 interviews: the same person could describe all three. They describe the material in this purposive sample, not prevalence among rural older people. A mention counted only where the participant described a concrete encounter or obstacle, rather than expressing a general opinion about public services.

Analysis showed that a correctly understood instruction could still be difficult to act on when the resident lacked transport, had to obtain another document or could not identify which office had responsibility. Conversely, staff explanation sometimes resolved an immediate misunderstanding without changing the procedure itself. These distinctions informed the separation of comprehension, procedural burden and service outcome in the final coding framework.

## Limitations and completed outputs

The study did not link interviews to clinical records, independently verify completed referrals or measure changes in wellbeing. It cannot estimate a causal care-access benefit. Completer analysis may overstate or understate change if the participants without follow-up differed in relevant ways. Recruitment through service centres also missed residents who had no contact with those centres.

Cultural participation was not a structured exposure in the study. References to libraries, associations or local events arose incidentally in some narratives, without a common question sequence or a reliable denominator. No cultural intervention or cultural trial took place.

Completed outputs include a restricted interview corpus, the scoring rubric, a coding manual, published analyses and an aggregate feedback note returned to participating service managers. Receipt of that note was documented; implementation of its observations was not evaluated. Public release covered the blank instruments and aggregate tables, not identifiable transcripts or audio.

# Final scientific summary: Palabras de ventanilla y cuidados rurales

**Issued 18 March 2026; administrative status checked 24 September 2026**

English working version prepared for international scholarly exchange.

Project period: 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025. Funding: Programa Aragonés de Investigación sobre Servicios de Proximidad, regional award PAISP-2022-017. Total awarded funding: EUR 184,000, comprising EUR 120,000 administered by Instituto de Estudios Cívicos de Valdemora and EUR 64,000 administered by Universidad de Valdencina.

Overall scientific coordinator: Dr Berta Lascuén Aroza, Instituto de Estudios Cívicos de Valdemora. Language-assessment work-package lead: Dr Maite Sorell Valdeza, Universidad de Valdencina. The project is complete. The regional office acknowledged receipt of the consolidated final report in March 2026.

## Purpose and setting

The project examined service language, administrative procedures and the practical work older rural residents undertake when seeking care-related information. Its empirical focus was residents' accounts of encounters and their ability to interpret information about an appointment, a supporting document or a referral.

Participating centres were local service points providing care-related information, nursing contact or administrative assistance. Their functions included both community-facing advice and care coordination. Access was negotiated separately at each centre. The coordinating institute managed cross-institution administration; the university managed the language instruments and the university-held interview corpus.

## Sample and procedures

The completed 2025 field study interviewed 90 rural residents aged 65 or older across 15 service centres. Recruitment was purposive, with six interviewees at each centre. Centre staff circulated the approved information sheet, and researchers documented individual consent before enrolment. Participants were able to undertake an interview with the communication support available under the approved protocol.

Interviews were completed between February and May 2025. Each participant discussed a recent service encounter and completed an initial language-access assessment. A repeat assessment was offered four to six weeks later to examine score change across the participant's next routine centre contact. Routine contact could include explanation of an appointment, document requirement or referral. Staff explanations were not standardised, and the research team did not allocate an intervention. All repeat assessments were complete by July 2025.

The repeated task used equivalent service scenarios. Interviewers recorded participants' accounts of the intervening contact, but there was no independent verification of the content or duration of staff assistance. The assessment concerned interpretation of service information rather than whether treatment or an entitlement had been obtained.

Paired assessments were available for 72 participants, representing 80% of the interview sample. Of the remaining 18 participants, 11 declined the repeat assessment and seven could not be reached within the follow-up window. All initial interviews and assessments were retained under the participants' consent. No missing follow-up scores were imputed for the primary descriptive analysis.

## Instrument and analysis

The language-access score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating more successful interpretation and explanation of service information. Tasks covered identifying a required action, understanding a deadline, distinguishing a recommendation from a requirement, and explaining where clarification could be sought. The rubric was developed within the project; validation against health literacy, completed care access or wellbeing measures was not undertaken.

Two assessors independently scored 32 of the 162 assessment records before discussion of disagreements: 16 initial and 16 repeat assessments, selected across centres. Absolute-agreement reliability for a single assessor, estimated using a two-way random-effects intraclass correlation coefficient, was ICC 0.86 (95% CI 0.73–0.93). The scoring manual records the subsequent consensus decisions used in the analytic dataset.

The paired analysis estimated mean within-person score change among completers. Its confidence interval used resampling at centre level to reflect clustering. With only 15 centres, the interval remains sensitive to the observed centres. It describes sampling uncertainty under the analysis assumptions and excludes uncertainty from selection bias, differential attrition and unmeasured changes between assessments.

Two researchers independently coded 18 interviews before reconciliation. Cohen's kappa was 0.78 for language-related difficulties, 0.77 for administrative sequencing and 0.75 for transport. **University research governance memorandum, 24 September 2026**

Custodian: Dr Maite Sorell Valdeza, Universidad de Valdencina. This memorandum records the permissions attached to the completed rural service-language study, the materials retained and the institutional procedure for site access and participant enrolment.

## Existing permissions and materials

The university ethics committee approved the predecessor study under reference UV-CEI-2024-041 on 12 December 2024. Written site permissions covered the 15 participating service centres. Each of the 90 interview participants gave documented informed consent before enrolment, including consent to the interview, its recording, the assessments and the specified research use of the material.

The approved information sheet and consent process covered subsequent analysis of the interview corpus concerning language, administrative and territorial barriers in care-related service encounters. Secondary analysis within this scope is covered by UV-CEI-2024-041 and requires no further approval. This authorisation excludes new interviews, recontact for a different study, linkage to clinical records and unrestricted changes of research purpose.

The restricted corpus contains 90 interview transcripts and their associated audio, initial assessment records for all 90 participants and repeat assessment records for 72 participants. There are 162 assessment records in total. The 18 participants without repeat assessments remain represented by their initial assessments and interviews. Analytic files contain pseudonymous centre codes and research identifiers. Names and contact details are held separately. Access to the linkage key is limited to the designated custodian and authorised governance staff.

Some interviews contain incidental references to cultural or associational activities. The consent documents cover the approved service-encounter research purpose. They do not provide consent for a separate cultural-participation study. A material change of purpose requires a documented governance assessment and, where applicable, an ethics amendment or additional consent. The incidental references were collected without a common participation instrument and cannot constitute a validated participation measure.

## Site and consent registers

At 24 September 2026, the permission register contains entries only for the 15 centres under UV-CEI-2024-041. The consent register contains only the records of the 90 participants in that study. ## Procedure for new sites and participants

The institutional protocol prohibits recruitment into a new-centre study before both written permission from that centre and the person's documented informed consent are in place. Written permission must identify the authorised activity and the responsible site contact. Informal introductions and expressions of interest are recorded as correspondence, separately from the permission register.

Following written site permission and the applicable ethics approval, authorised site staff may circulate an approved information sheet. This information stage precedes enrolment. Researchers must provide an accessible explanation, establish that participation is voluntary and document consent before the person is recruited into the research sample or any research interview or assessment begins. Access to services must not depend on participation.

The protocol requires communication support appropriate to the person and a check that the explanation has been understood. Older age alone is not evidence of impaired decision-making capacity. Inclusion through proxy consent requires separate approved arrangements; the existing procedure covers participants providing their own consent.

## Storage, disclosure and analysis

Audio, transcripts and assessment files remain restricted. Pseudonymisation does not make them anonymous: combinations of village, service encounter and family circumstances can identify someone locally. Analysts remove unnecessary identifiers and review distinctive contextual details before using quotations. The custodian maintains the access register and records the purpose of each approved analyst's access.
